source.title: Temporal Recurrence Favors Fewer Layers
source.authors: Ivan Anokhin; Johan Obando-Ceron; Irina Rish; Sebastian Risi

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study experimentally examines loss and compute allocation in language models, but varies within-step depth, expert count and width rather than testing the stated parameter/token scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The FineWeb experiments report validation cross-entropy for recurrent and non-recurrent models under approximately matched per-token compute. They do not fit or test power laws in parameter count, training tokens or compute, nor do they test downstream-task predictability. The paper cites compute-optimal scaling as context, but its reported results are its own depth/parallel-capacity allocation experiments.
record.test_reason: The study compares recurrent and non-recurrent models on FineWeb (and Sokoban) by sweeping within-step depth, parallel expert count and width under approximately matched per-token compute. It fits no power law in parameters, tokens or compute, and does not test extrapolation, the compute-optimal parameter/token split, other-modality laws or downstream predictability. Hoffmann et al. is cited only as related work. The depth/width sweeps resemble V4, but they use non-standard parallel-expert blocks, a recurrence intervention and only 2–3 budgets near 1B tokens. No result is framed as testing whether shape matters little at fixed parameter count. The record's 'tests'/T2 is therefore too strong.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that temporal recurrence shifts the best observed compute allocation toward substantially fewer within-step layers, with comparable or better performance, in Sokoban and streamed FineWeb. Per-layer expert count and width remain useful ways to spend compute.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses matched-compute allocation sweeps over depth, expert count and width, with or without temporal recurrence; it does not use the parameter/token/compute power-law fitting approach described in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The preferred depth varies with recurrence and tested setting; the paper reports results across compute budgets and attention-window lengths. It also notes that architecture-specific choices and recurrent training stabilization may affect allocations.

fits_no_version.finding: Under approximately matched per-token compute on about 1B FineWeb tokens, recurrent Transformers reach their best observed validation loss at L=2–4. Non-recurrent Transformers keep improving up to L=16–32. In the small budget, a recurrent L=2 model (about 3.51) matches the best non-recurrent model at L=16.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Temporal recurrence shifts the loss-minimising compute allocation toward fewer within-step layers and more parallel capacity.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched compute, non-recurrent parallel-expert Transformers are strongly depth-sensitive: shallow L=1 allocations reach about 3.96–4.03 versus about 3.51 at L=16 (Fig. 5). This is far from the 'shape matters little' picture, but involves extreme parallel-expert configurations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Replacing depth with dense parallel experts at matched compute costs substantial loss in non-recurrent Transformers.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says code is available at fewer-layers-with-rec but gives no URL.
record.problems: The study covers a restricted range of architectures, compute budgets, training durations and tasks; reported allocations are the best among those evaluated, not globally compute-optimal. Compute is approximately matched by a proxy rather than measured as realized hardware efficiency. Recurrent and non-recurrent architectures are not perfectly matched, and recurrent Transformers use additional stabilization and memory-management choices.
record.rows_left_out: No further FineWeb loss-allocation results were extracted from the allocation-sweep figures in Appendix I (Figures 14 and 15); those figures provide additional configurations but do not report power-law fits or parameter/token compute-optimal trends. Sokoban results were omitted because the claim concerns language-model pretraining loss.

untested.parts: Power-law fall of loss with parameters, tokens or compute over several orders of magnitude. Only 2–3 compute budgets are run, with no fit.
Extrapolation from small fitted runs to much larger runs.
How the loss-minimising parameter count and token count grow with compute. Tokens are held fixed at about 1B.
Effect of depth/width aspect ratio of standard Transformers at fixed parameter count. The sweeps use parallel-expert blocks under matched compute and are not posed as a test of this.
Power laws in other modalities or regimes. The Sokoban RL results contain no scaling-law fits.
Downstream task predictability from scale or loss.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup choices.

record.verdict_notes: The record's relation (tests/T2) contradicts its own gate note and its all-'not_tested' version statuses. The relation is corrected to cites_only/T6. The only near-contact is with V4. If curators consider dense parallel-expert depth/width trade-offs at matched compute (parameters roughly proportional to compute here) to fall within V4, the non-recurrent FineWeb sweeps (Figs. 5, 14, 15) would show large loss changes from very shallow allocations. That would fall outside Kaplan's 'wide range', so at most limits_scope. I did not label it, because the paper does not frame or measure it as a shape-at-fixed-parameters test.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law loss dependence on parameter count, tokens or compute, including behavior over several orders of magnitude.
Extrapolation from small runs to substantially larger runs.
The parameter-count/token split and whether either grows as a stable power of compute.
Architecture effects at fixed parameter count; the study varies architecture allocations under approximately matched compute.
Other modalities and training regimes beyond streamed FineWeb language modeling.
Downstream-task performance and its predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted scaling exponents or parameter/token compute-optimal splits on fitting choices, and departures from single power laws.
